text.content:
The eldest Tzimisce of the Carpathian line still spoken of by name, Yorak assumed the mantle of Voivode when the clan's Antediluvian — the Eldest — fell into torpor following an attack by the Salubri knight Samiel. Reputedly the first koldun, Yorak withdrew into the caves where the demon-spirit Kupala whispered loudest, spending centuries enslaving tribes of Slavs, Celts, and Thracians for his experiments and pursuing Azhi Dahaka, the ecstatic transcendence at the heart of the Path of Metamorphosis. His magnum opus, the Cathedral of Flesh, was a subterranean palace of living architecture — pillars of grafted bodies, walls of singing mouths, windows of stretched and preserved skin — built over centuries with thousands of victims, and became the center of Metamorphosist thought and worship. No one now knows where it stood; where it once rose, only a gaping hole remains.

Uninterested in kingship, Yorak instead Embraced influential tribal leaders and let them handle politics on his behalf, most famously the shaman-goddess Shaagra. He reputedly fell during the chaos of the Anarch Revolt, though the culprit remains a mystery even to his own clan.

A Slavic shaman of the Vroi tribe who ruled her people as goddess, leader, and mystic before Yorak Embraced her, passing over rivals Triglav the Three-Headed and Lambach Ruthven in the process (a slight Lambach never forgot). Shaagra's Embrace precipitated the Tzimisce practice of claiming stock from noble families and tribal leaders to influence the region's mortals, giving rise to the revenant families. She never knew her sire, and once trained in Tzimisce ways and bound by blood oath, she and her tribe followed her granddaughter and favored ghoul, Libuse, into the Danube Plain, eventually settling land that would become Prague — the westernmost point of Carpathian Tzimisce influence and, later, a flashpoint of the Tremere-Tzimisce conflict. Shaagra herself slept in fitful torpor in Kupala-tainted soil, growing steadily more insane with the passing centuries.

A Methuselah of ancient Carpathian nobility, passed over for Shaagra's Embrace in favor of Triglav the Three-Headed and never forgetting the insult. Despite that old grudge, Lambach attended Kupala's Eve when the young Tzimisce broke their sires' blood oaths, and unlike many elders never turned against the anarchs who did it — without his vitae, many Fiends doubt they could have broken their bonds at all. Other Sabbat dismiss him as a fool and a screw-up, but those who have dealt with him longer suspect he plays that role deliberately, the better to observe unnoticed.

Lambach has reputedly witnessed the Eldest itself twice in recent history: once when the diablerist Lugoj Blood-breaker attempted to drain it, and once beneath the streets of New York. Some among the clan whisper that this is no coincidence — that Lambach is, unknowingly, the Eldest's chronicler, kept alive by fragments of its strength precisely so that he might document the clan's actions while his sire's sire slumbers, and that he will survive until the Eldest's final awakening.

Descended from Noriz, the so-called Corrupter of Legions, Lugoj became the first voice of Tzimisce dissent against the clan's elders, vowing alongside his siblings never to be anyone's pawn again. Together with his ally Velya the Flayer, Lugoj spent decades searching the Carpathians for Kupala's sacred fire-flower, an artifact the young Tzimisce hoped would shatter the blood bonds their sires held over them. When the pair found it, they gathered their fellow rebels on Kupala's Eve, broke the ancient bonds, and set the Tzimisce Anarch Revolt into motion.

Some accounts claim Lugoj later committed the Amaranth upon the torpid Eldest itself, only for the Antediluvian to turn the act back on him — meaning that Lugoj, now himself in torpor somewhere in the Carpathians, may in some sense be the Eldest reborn. Other, more skeptical elders insist Lugoj was merely the Eldest's chosen instrument all along, guided to the fire-flower (in truth a fragment of the Antediluvian's own flesh) so that it could sunder its progeny's old alliances and remake the clan's loyalties around itself once more.

Claimed by his followers to be the first childe of the Tzimisce Antediluvian itself, the Dracon was a principal founder of Constantinople and, unlike his Carpathian kin, spoke out publicly against Kupala and the koldunic sorcery bound up with it. His disputes with the Balkan Tzimisce turned to open war after his grandchilde Gesu suffered a mysterious torpor the Dracon blamed on his Carpathian cousins; in retaliation, he ambushed the koldun Triglav the Three-Headed and deprived him of his namesake heads, while the Balkan Tzimisce destroyed Byzantine Akoimetai monasteries in reply. That rift, which brought the Obertus revenant family into the clan's service as reparation, has never fully healed, even in the modern nights.

The Dracon's spiritual heirs, the Children of the Dracon, style themselves a knightly order atoning for some unnamed sin the clan committed — possibly Kupala's Night itself — and reject koldunic sorcery even as they remain within the Sabbat, opposing nearly every policy the clan Voivode enacts. The Dracon himself has not been seen in the Final Nights; some Tzimisce believe he simply grew tired of Constantinople's fall and vanished into the wider Jyhad.

Not a Cainite at all, but a demon-spirit of the land itself, bound by ancient Lupine shamans deep within the Carpathians — the mountains were said to have been raised by their claws specifically to imprison it. When the Tzimisce Antediluvian learned to speak to Kupala through dreams, the two struck a bargain: the Eldest would free Kupala from its prison in exchange for magic and allegiance against their shared Lupine enemies. The pact succeeded, but Kupala remained bound to the soil of the Carpathians even after its release, unable to return to whatever hell or spirit-realm once claimed it. It took the mountains as its new domain instead, sharing its existence — and its madness — with the Tzimisce ever since.

Kupala is the source of the clan's practice of koldunic sorcery, its curse of ancestral soil dependence, and (some koldun believe) the reason the Tzimisce sleep uneasily even in their own homeland: their rituals do not ward off Kupala's influence so much as earn the demon's favor for being obedient. Kupala is widely blamed for corrupting the soil of Eastern Europe and for the strange fertility of Tzimisce sorcery in the modern nights, when so many neonates who should have no access to the old ways have somehow rediscovered them.
